title: Breast cancer: with AI, mammograms can bring forward diagnosis by up to six years
source_used: Il Sole 24 ORE (English edition); RSNA press release read for the study details
key_facts: A Swedish study published in the journal Radiology applied three commercially available AI computer-aided detection systems to mammograms from the VAI-B database.
It covered 88,963 mammograms from 31,394 patients taken between January 2008 and April 2019 in four Swedish regions.
At 90% specificity the systems flagged up to 19.7% of those later diagnosed with breast cancer six years before diagnosis, up to 25.2% four years before, and up to 39.3% two years before.
Study leader Fredrik Strand of Karolinska University Hospital in Stockholm said around 20% of breast cancer cases show signs visible to AI some six years before diagnosis.

Massimo Calabrese, director of the Oncology and Breast Radiology Unit at Policlinico San Martino in Genoa, warns the study is retrospective and that spotting signs after the fact does not mean a tumour could have been diagnosed six years earlier.
He says it must still be shown that this ability translates into real clinical benefit for women.
The Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) press release on the study is listed by Google News as 9 Jun 2026.
quote_evidence: “Around 20 per cent of breast cancer cases show mammographic signs that are already visible to AI some six years before diagnosis,” Strand commented in a statement.

Above all, it will be necessary to demonstrate that this predictive capability can translate into a real clinical benefit for women
why_it_matters_hint: AI might one day help pick out women who need closer screening, but this looks back at old scans and no benefit to women has been shown.
